module_title: Getting Started with Wheat & Barley in Africa

lessons.title: Why Wheat and Barley Matter for African Markets
lessons.body: Africa imports over 40 million tonnes of wheat each year, costing more than $15 billion. That's a massive opportunity for local farmers. Countries like Egypt, Nigeria, Ethiopia, and South Africa are among the world's top wheat importers. But only a fraction is grown locally. For example, Nigeria imports about 5 million tonnes annually, while local production is under 100,000 tonnes. This gap means millers and food processors are desperate for local grain. Barley is also in high demand, especially for beer production. Africa's beer market is growing at 5% per year, and breweries like Heineken, Diageo, and SABMiller source barley locally when possible. In Ethiopia, barley is a traditional crop used for food and local beer (tella). The African Development Bank estimates that import substitution in wheat could create 5 million jobs. For you as a small-scale farmer, this means if you can produce quality grain, you have a ready market. You don't need to export; you can sell to local millers, breweries, or feedlots. The key is to understand that wheat and barley are not just cropsâthey are strategic commodities that African governments want to support. Many countries offer subsidies, improved seeds, and extension services. By growing these crops, you contribute to food security and earn good money. Start small, but think big: one hectare of wheat can yield 3-5 tonnes, and with a price of $300 per tonne, that's $900-$1,500 per harvest. Barley yields similar but often sells for $250-$400 per tonne. The demand is there. Your job is to meet it.

lessons.title: Identifying Local Demand: Bread, Malt, and Animal Feed
lessons.body: Before you plant, find out who will buy your grain. There are three main markets: bread, malt, and animal feed. Bread is the biggest. In cities like Nairobi, Lagos, and Cairo, bakeries run daily. A single large bakery can use 10 tonnes of wheat flour per day. That flour comes from millers. So your target is the miller, not the bakery directly. Millers like United Milling in Kenya or Flour Mills of Nigeria buy thousands of tonnes. They prefer consistent quality: protein content of 11-13% for bread wheat, moisture below 12%, and low foreign matter. Visit your local miller and ask about their requirements. For malt, breweries need barley with specific qualities: high germination, low protein (9-11%), and uniform size. In South Africa, SAB (now AB InBev) contracts farmers directly. In Ethiopia, breweries like BGI Ethiopia buy local barley. If you are near a brewery, that's a golden opportunity. Animal feed is the third market. Feedlots and poultry farms use wheat and barley as energy sources. They often buy lower-grade grain that doesn't meet milling or malting standards. This is a good fallback if your crop has defects. To identify demand, talk to: 1) Millers (look for 'roller mills' or 'flour mills' in your area). 2) Breweries (check for 'maltings' or 'breweries'). 3) Feedlots (large cattle or poultry operations). Also check with local traders and cooperatives. Attend farmer field days and agricultural shows. Ask about prices, volumes, and contract terms. A simple phone call to a miller can save you months of guesswork. Remember: demand is local. Don't assume you must sell to a big city. A small feedlot 20 km away might be your best customer.

lessons.title: Choosing Between Wheat and Barley for Your Farm
lessons.body: Wheat and barley look similar but have different needs and markets. Your choice depends on climate, soil, and market access. Wheat prefers cooler temperatures (15-25Â°C) and well-drained loam soil. It is sensitive to heat stress during flowering. Barley is tougher: it tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil better. Barley grows from 6Â°C to 30Â°C, though optimal is 15-20Â°C. In Africa, wheat is grown in highlands like the Ethiopian Highlands, Kenyan Rift Valley, and South African Free State. Barley is grown in similar areas but also in drier regions like Morocco, Tunisia, and parts of Kenya. If you have irrigation, wheat can be grown in lowlands during cool season. If you rely on rain, barley is safer in areas with erratic rainfall. Soil: both need pH 6.0-7.5. Wheat needs more nitrogen (100-150 kg/ha) than barley (60-100 kg/ha). Barley matures faster (90-120 days) than wheat (120-150 days). That means barley fits better in short rainy seasons. Market: wheat has higher demand but also more competition from imports. Barley has niche markets (malting) that pay premium if quality is high. In Ethiopia, barley for local beer (tella) sells well. In Kenya, wheat for bread is king. Consider your resources: If you have fertile land and reliable rain, wheat may give higher returns. If your land is marginal or rainfall is low, barley is more reliable. Also think about rotation: barley is often used in rotation with legumes. A simple decision tool: 1) Check your altitude. Above 1,800 m, both work. Below 1,200 m, barley is better. 2) Check your market. If a brewery is within 50 km, consider barley. If a miller is nearby, consider wheat. 3) Check your budget. Barley needs less fertilizer and fewer pesticides. Start with a small plot of each to see what works. Many farmers grow both to spread risk.

lessons.title: Understanding African Climates: Highlands vs. Lowlands
lessons.body: Africa's climate varies hugely. For wheat and barley, altitude matters more than latitude. Highlands (above 1,500 m) are cooler and often have reliable rainfall. Lowlands (below 1,000 m) are hotter and drier. Wheat thrives in highlands. In Ethiopia, wheat is grown at 1,800-2,800 m. In Kenya, the Rift Valley (1,800-2,500 m) is the wheat belt. In South Africa, the Free State (1,200-1,800 m) is key. Barley is more flexible. It grows in highlands but also in lowlands with irrigation or winter rain. In Morocco, barley is grown in lowlands (0-500 m) with 300-500 mm rainfall. In Egypt, barley is grown in the Nile Delta (lowland) in winter. Temperature: Wheat needs a cool growing season. If temperatures exceed 30Â°C during grain filling, yields drop. Barley can handle up to 35Â°C. Rainfall: Wheat needs 400-600 mm well-distributed. Barley needs 300-500 mm. In lowlands, you need irrigation. For example, in Nigeria's savannah, wheat is grown under irrigation in the dry season (November-March) when temperatures are cooler. Soil: Highlands often have acidic soils (pH 4.5-5.5). You may need to add lime. Lowlands have more alkaline soils. Test your soil before planting. Tools: Use a simple soil test kit (cost $20) or send samples to a lab. Also consider frost: Wheat is more frost-tolerant than barley at flowering. In highlands like Lesotho, frost can kill barley. Practical tips: 1) Find your altitude using a GPS or phone app. 2) Check local weather records for temperature and rainfall. 3) Talk to neighbors about what they grow. 4) If you are in a lowland area, choose barley with irrigation. 5) If you are in a highland area, wheat is usually better. Remember: climate change is making rainfall less predictable. Drought-tolerant barley varieties are a safe bet in many areas.

lessons.title: Basic Costs and Potential Profits in Small-Scale Farming
lessons.body: Let's talk money. For one hectare of wheat or barley, you need to budget for inputs, labour, and equipment. Seed: Wheat seed costs about $30-$50 per hectare. Barley seed is similar, $25-$45. Use certified seed for better yields. Fertilizer: Wheat needs 100 kg N, 50 kg P, and 50 kg K per hectare. That's about $150-$200. Barley needs less: 60 kg N, 40 kg P, 40 kg K, about $100-$150. Herbicides and pesticides: $50-$100 for wheat, $30-$70 for barley. Labour: Land preparation, planting, weeding, harvesting. In most African countries, manual labour costs $100-$200 per hectare. If you use oxen or a tractor, add $50-$100. Harvesting and threshing: $50-$100. Total costs: Wheat: $380-$650 per hectare. Barley: $280-$500 per hectare. Yields: With good management, wheat yields 3-5 tonnes per hectare in highlands. Barley yields 2.5-4 tonnes. Prices: Wheat farmgate price in Africa ranges from $250-$400 per tonne. Barley: $200-$350 per tonne. But malting barley can fetch $400-$500. Revenue: Wheat: 4 tonnes x $300 = $1,200. Barley: 3 tonnes x $250 = $750. Profit: Wheat: $1,200 - $500 = $700 per hectare. Barley: $750 - $400 = $350. But if you get malting contract, barley profit can be $800+. These are estimates. Your actual costs and yields depend on your location and management. To improve profits: 1) Use improved seeds. 2) Apply fertilizer correctly. 3) Control weeds early. 4) Harvest on time to avoid losses. 5) Sell in bulk to get better prices. 6) Consider value addition (e.g., milling your own flour). Start with 0.5 hectare to learn. Keep records of every expense and income. After one season, you'll know your real numbers. Many farmers double yields by simply planting on time and weeding twice.

lessons.title: Finding Your First Buyers: Millers, Breweries, and Feedlots
lessons.body: You've grown your crop. Now you need to sell it. Start earlyâbefore harvest. Identify buyers in your area. Millers: Look for flour mills. In Kenya, major millers include Unga Group, Pembe, and Jogoo. In Nigeria, Flour Mills of Nigeria, Honeywell, and Dangote. In Ethiopia, Ada Flour Mill. Visit their buying centers. Ask for the procurement officer. They will tell you quality standards and price. Often they buy through cooperatives or aggregators. Join a cooperative to access these buyers. Breweries: If you grow barley, contact breweries. In South Africa, AB InBev (SAB) contracts farmers. In Ethiopia, BGI Ethiopia, Dashen, and Habesha breweries buy local barley. In Kenya, East African Breweries (EABL) sources barley from farmers in the Rift Valley. They often provide seed and extension support. Feedlots: Large cattle feedlots and poultry farms buy grain. In South Africa, feedlots like Karan Beef buy thousands of tonnes. In Zimbabwe, Irvine's and Colcom. In Nigeria, Chi Farms and Olam. They may buy lower grades. To find buyers: 1) Ask your extension officer. 2) Attend agricultural trade shows. 3) Search online for 'flour mills in [your country]' or 'breweries in [your region]'. 4) Call the buyer and introduce yourself. 5) Offer a sample. 6) Negotiate a contract before planting. A contract gives you guaranteed price and market. But read the fine print: quality specs, delivery terms, payment schedule. If you can't get a contract, sell to local traders. They pay less but are flexible. Avoid selling immediately after harvest when prices are low. Store your grain properly (dry, clean, pest-free) and sell later when prices rise. A simple storage method: use hermetic bags (e.g., Purdue Improved Crop Storage bags) to prevent weevils. With good storage, you can wait 3-6 months for better prices. Remember: your reputation matters. Deliver clean, dry grain on time. That's how you build a long-term relationship with buyers.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Getting Started with Wheat & Barley in Africa

This lesson is your desk reference. It pulls together the numbers, contacts, and decision rules you need before you commit seed, land, or money to wheat or barley. Everything here is written for the smallholder or emerging commercial farmer who intends to sell, not just grow. Treat the tables as planning tools, the diagram as your route map from field to buyer, and the checklist as your go/no-go gate.

Across Africa, wheat and barley sit at the centre of two of the fastest-growing food and beverage value chains. Wheat feeds the bread, pasta, and biscuit market; barley feeds the beer, malt, and animal feed market. Demand is rising faster than local production in most countries, which is why millers and breweries import heavily and why governments in Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania, and Zambia run import-substitution programmes that pay real premiums to local growers who can meet quality specs.

1. The Route from Your Field to a Paying Buyer

Before you plough, map the chain. The diagram below shows the standard flow for both crops in African markets, including the quality gate that decides whether you get a premium or a discount.

2. Wheat vs. Barley: Decision Data

Use the table below to compare the two crops on the variables that decide profitability in African conditions. Figures are indicative ranges drawn from published extension and industry data; your local extension officer or buyer contract will give exact numbers for your district.

Table 1: Wheat vs. Barley â Agronomic and Market Comparison for African Smallholders
Factor Wheat Barley
Typical yield (smallholder, rain-fed)1.5â3.0 t/ha1.5â2.5 t/ha
Typical yield (irrigated / high input)4.0â6.0 t/ha3.5â5.0 t/ha
Altitude preference1,800â2,800 m (highlands)1,500â3,000 m (highlands, more cold-tolerant)
Rainfall / irrigation need450â650 mm, irrigation preferred400â550 mm, more drought-tolerant
Soil pH6.0â7.56.0â8.0 (more tolerant of alkalinity)
Days to maturity110â150 days90â130 days
Main buyerMillers (bread, pasta, biscuits)Breweries, maltsters, feedlots
Key quality specProtein 11â13%, moisture <13%Plump kernels >85%, moisture <12.5%
Indicative farmgate price (2024, USD/t)280â420220â350
Contract availabilityStrong in Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria, ZambiaStrong in Ethiopia, South Africa, Kenya (malting)
Storage riskModerate (weevil, moisture)Moderateâhigh (must stay dry for malt)
Sources: FAO (2023), FAOSTAT Crop Production Data; CIMMYT (2022), Wheat in Africa; ICARDA (2021), Barley Improvement in Dry Areas; Ethiopia Ministry of Agriculture (2023), Wheat Sector Strategy.

3. Start-Up Costs and Potential Returns (1 Hectare, Small-Scale)

The table below models a single hectare of rain-fed wheat or barley in an African highland context. It assumes you already have access to land (owned or rented) and basic tools. Costs are in USD and reflect 2024 regional averages; adjust to your country.

Table 2: Indicative Start-Up Budget and Returns per Hectare (2024 USD)
Cost Item Wheat (USD) Barley (USD) Notes
Certified seed60â9050â80Use improved varieties from registered seed growers
Fertiliser (NPS + urea)180â260150â220Split application recommended
Land preparation (tractor hire)80â12080â120Higher if manual labour only
Labour (planting, weeding, harvest)150â220130â200Family labour can reduce cash cost
Crop protection40â7030â60Herbicides, fungicides as needed
Harvest & threshing60â10060â100Mechanical or manual
Transport & bags40â7040â70Depends on distance to buyer
Total cash cost610â930540â850â
Expected yield (t/ha)2.0â3.01.8â2.5Rain-fed, moderate inputs
Farmgate price (USD/t)280â420220â350Contract vs. spot market
Gross revenue560â1,260396â875â
Net margin (range)â50 to +650â154 to +335Negative if yield <1.5 t/ha or price is low
Sources: Compiled from FAO (2023), FAOSTAT; CIMMYT (2022), Wheat in Africa; ICARDA (2021), Barley Improvement in Dry Areas; and Ethiopia Ministry of Agriculture (2023), Wheat Sector Strategy. Prices vary widely by country and season.

Business reading: Wheat offers a higher revenue ceiling but demands more water and fertiliser. Barley is cheaper to grow and more drought-tolerant, but its price is lower unless you are on a malting contract. The margin is thin at low yields â your first job is to get above 2 t/ha, not to expand area.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Aflatoxin and Storage Mould

Never sell or feed mouldy grain. Wheat and barley stored above 13% moisture can develop Aspergillus moulds that produce aflatoxins â invisible poisons that cause liver cancer and are strictly regulated in export and milling contracts. In Africa, aflatoxin contamination has blocked maize and groundnut exports and is increasingly tested in wheat and barley.

  • Dry grain to below 12.5% moisture before storage. Use a moisture meter â do not guess.
  • Store on pallets, never directly on bare earth or against damp walls.
  • Never mix mouldy grain with clean grain to "dilute" it. This spreads contamination and can void your entire contract.
  • Wear a dust mask when handling mouldy grain; aflatoxin dust is hazardous to breathe.
  • If you suspect mould, get a lab test before selling. A failed test is better than a rejected truckload and a blacklisted buyer relationship.

Reference: FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius maximum levels for mycotoxins in cereals; African Union (2016), Sanitary and Phytosanitary Standards Framework.

4. Matching Crop to Climate: Highlands vs. Lowlands

Most of Africa's wheat and barley is grown in the highlands â Ethiopia's Arsi and Bale zones, Kenya's Rift Valley, Tanzania's Southern Highlands, Zimbabwe's Eastern Highlands, and South Africa's Free State. These areas offer cool nights, reliable rainfall, and lower pest pressure. Lowland production is possible only with irrigation and heat-tolerant varieties, and is usually a commercial-scale play, not a smallholder one.

Rule of thumb: If you are below 1,500 m altitude and cannot irrigate, choose another crop. If you are between 1,500 and 1,800 m, barley is the safer bet. Above 1,800 m, both crops work; choose based on your nearest buyer.

5. Finding Your First Buyers

Do not plant a single hectare until you have had a conversation with at least one buyer. Here is who to approach and what they want:

  • Millers: Want consistent protein, low moisture, and clean grain. In Ethiopia, the Ethiopian Millers Association and the Ethiopian Grain Trade Enterprise are key contacts. In Kenya, approach Unga Group, Pembe Flour Mills, or Capwell Industries. In Nigeria, Flour Mills of Nigeria and Honeywell Flour Mills run local sourcing programmes.
  • Breweries and maltsters: Want plump, low-protein barley with high germination. In Ethiopia, BGI Ethiopia and Heineken's Kilinto malt plant contract growers. In Kenya, Kenya Breweries Limited (EABL) sources through its subsidiary. In South Africa, SABMiller/AB InBev contracts through Southern Associated Maltsters.
  • Feedlots and feed mills: Buy both crops as energy feed, often at a discount to milling grade. They are a good fallback buyer if your grain misses malting or milling spec. Look for large poultry integrators and dairy cooperatives in your region.
  • Cooperatives and aggregators: If you cannot meet a buyer's minimum volume, join a cooperative that can. Many contract schemes only deal with groups of 20+ farmers.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Buyer first: Secure a verbal or written buyer commitment before planting. No buyer = no crop.
  2. Test your soil: Get a soil test for pH, organic matter, and phosphorus. Wheat and barley need pH 6.0â7.5.
  3. Choose certified seed: Buy improved, disease-resistant varieties from a registered seed grower â not grain from last year's harvest.
  4. Check altitude and water: Confirm you are above 1,500 m or have irrigation. Below that, switch to a more suitable crop.
  5. Budget the full cash cost: Land prep, seed, fertiliser, labour, harvest, transport. Do not underestimate labour.
  6. Plan drying and storage: Target <12.5% moisture. Invest in tarpaulins, pallets, and a moisture meter.
  7. Know your quality spec: Ask your buyer for the exact moisture, protein, and foreign matter limits in writing.
  8. Join a cooperative or contract scheme: It solves aggregation, input credit, and market access in one move.

Further Reading

  • FAO FAOSTAT â Crop Production Data (free): official yield and area statistics for wheat and barley by African country.
  • CIMMYT â International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (free): wheat research, varieties, and value chain reports for Africa.
  • ICARDA â International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (free): barley improvement, drought-tolerant varieties, and dryland farming guides.
  • African Union â Department of Agriculture, Rural Development, Blue Economy and Sustainable Environment (free): continental agricultural policy, SPS standards, and market frameworks.
  • African Development Bank â Feed Africa Strategy (free): financing and value chain development reports for cereal crops.

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills course Wheat & Barley Farming. Always verify prices, varieties, and buyer requirements with your national extension service and local buyer before committing resources.

quiz.q: Approximately how much wheat does Africa import each year?
quiz.explanation: Africa imports over 40 million tonnes of wheat annually, costing over $15 billion.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a major use of barley in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Barley is in high demand for beer production, especially by breweries like Heineken and Diageo.

quiz.q: What is the typical protein content required for bread wheat?
quiz.explanation: Millers prefer bread wheat with 11-13% protein content for good baking quality.

quiz.q: Which market often buys lower-grade grain that doesn't meet milling or malting standards?
quiz.explanation: Feedlots and poultry farms use wheat and barley as energy sources and often buy lower-grade grain.

quiz.q: What is the optimal temperature range for wheat growth?
quiz.explanation: Wheat prefers cooler temperatures (15-25Â°C) and is sensitive to heat stress during flowering.

quiz.q: Which crop is more tolerant to heat and drought?
quiz.explanation: Barley tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil better than wheat.

quiz.q: What is the typical pH range for both wheat and barley?
quiz.explanation: Both crops need a soil pH between 6.0 and 7.5 for optimal growth.

quiz.q: Which crop generally matures faster?
options: C) Both mature at the same time
quiz.explanation: Barley matures in 90-120 days, while wheat takes 120-150 days.

quiz.q: In Africa, wheat is best grown in which altitude range?
quiz.explanation: Wheat thrives in highlands above 1,500 m, such as the Ethiopian Highlands and Kenyan Rift Valley.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key consideration when choosing between wheat and barley?
quiz.explanation: Market access, climate, and soil type are all important factors in choosing between wheat and barley.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of certified wheat seed per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Certified wheat seed costs about $30-$50 per hectare.

quiz.q: How much nitrogen does barley typically need per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Barley needs less nitrogen (60-100 kg/ha) than wheat (100-150 kg/ha).

quiz.q: What is a typical yield for wheat in African highlands with good management?
quiz.explanation: With good management, wheat yields 3-5 tonnes per hectare in highlands.

quiz.q: Which of the following can increase profits for small-scale wheat farmers?
quiz.explanation: Using improved seeds is one of the recommended ways to improve profits.

quiz.q: What is a good storage method to prevent weevils in stored grain?
quiz.explanation: Hermetic bags, such as Purdue Improved Crop Storage bags, prevent weevils.

quiz.q: Which organization is a major buyer of barley in Ethiopia?
quiz.explanation: BGI Ethiopia is a major brewery that buys local barley in Ethiopia.

quiz.q: What is the first step to finding buyers for your grain?
options: C) Sell to the first trader you meet
quiz.explanation: It is important to identify buyers before harvest to secure a market.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a benefit of joining a cooperative?
options: D) No need for quality control
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives can help farmers access better markets and negotiate better prices.

quiz.q: What is malting barley typically used for?
quiz.explanation: Malting barley is used for beer production.

quiz.q: Which region in Kenya is known for wheat production?
quiz.explanation: The Rift Valley is the wheat belt in Kenya.

quiz.q: What is the typical rainfall requirement for barley?
quiz.explanation: Barley needs 300-500 mm of rainfall, less than wheat.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a tool for determining soil pH?
quiz.explanation: Both soil test kits and pH meters can be used to determine soil pH.

quiz.q: What is a common contract term to check before signing with a buyer?
quiz.explanation: Quality specs, delivery terms, and payment schedule are all important contract terms.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a lowland area where barley is grown?
quiz.explanation: Barley is grown in the Nile Delta (lowland) in winter.

quiz.q: What is the approximate farmgate price for wheat in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Wheat farmgate price in Africa ranges from $250-$400 per tonne.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a way to add value to your wheat?
quiz.explanation: Milling your own flour is a form of value addition that can increase profits.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of growing barley in marginal land?
quiz.explanation: Barley is more drought tolerant and can grow in marginal land.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a major wheat importer in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa are all among the world's top wheat importers.

quiz.q: What is the recommended practice to avoid selling at low prices after harvest?
options: B) Store grain properly and sell later
quiz.explanation: Storing grain properly and selling later when prices rise can improve profits.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a benefit of crop rotation with legumes?
quiz.explanation: Legumes in rotation fix nitrogen and improve soil fertility.
